paras: The threatened lynching of Jed Pritteheft was a reported plan by a large crowd of citizens of 'Pittsburgh county' to lynch Pritteheft, a Black man accused of assaulting an eight-year-old girl, around December 26, 1888. No attack on him was reported; he was taken to jail at Lynchburg, Virginia, and the episode survives only as one paragraph in the Richmond Dispatch.

According to a Lynchburg special telegram, Pritteheft was accused of assaulting an eight-year-old daughter of W. C. Pollock, who lived on Sandy creek in what the paper printed as 'Pittsburgh county'. The dispatch called him 'the negro desperado' and stated the assault as fact rather than as a charge.

Pritteheft had been captured 'a few days since' near Durham. Sheriff Overby then brought him to Lynchburg and committed him to jail. The dispatch added that it was 'understood a large crowd of citizens of Pittsburgh had intended to lynch him last night', but it described no gathering, attempt on the jail or harm to the prisoner.

The timing is uncertain, because the paper is dated December 27 while the dispatch dateline reads December 28. Read against the issue date, the dispatch places his arrival in Lynchburg and the planned lynching around December 25-26.
The coverage does not show whether Pritteheft was tried or what became of the charge against him.

The only report found was a short closing paragraph in a Richmond Dispatch telegram from Lynchburg whose headline, 'Took Laudanum', concerned a hotel suicide, with 'Escaped Lynching' as the last line of the deck. The paragraph adopted the accusation in its own voice, naming Pritteheft as the man 'who committed an assault', and reported the crowd's plan as hearsay without comment on it.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Jed Pritteheft
bases: The only report says a large crowd of citizens had intended to lynch Pritteheft, a jailed man accused of assault, though no attack on him is reported (A1).

Pritteheft was not killed: the dispatch reports only that a 'large crowd of citizens' had intended to lynch him over an alleged assault, and that he was committed to jail at Lynchburg (A1). It is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.
Only one paragraph in one paper, a Lynchburg special telegram to the Richmond Dispatch, reports the episode, and the planned lynching itself is given only as 'understood' (A1).

conflicts.note: A dispatch cannot postdate its paper; the dateline is probably a misprint or misreading, so the event falls about December 25-26, 1888.
